'''Arthur William Conway''' <small>{{post-nominals|FRS|size=100%}}<ref name="WhittakerObit">{{Cite journal | last1 = Whittaker | first1 = E. T. | author-link = E. T. Whittaker| title = Arthur William Conway. 1875–1950 | doi = 10.1098/rsbm.1951.0004  | doi-access = free| journal = [[Obituary Notices of Fellows of the Royal Society]] | volume = 7 | issue = 20 | pages =  328–340| year = 1951 }}</ref> [[Royal Irish Academy#Presidents|PRIA]]</small> (2 October 1875 – 11 July 1950) was a distinguished Irish mathematician and [[mathematical physicist]] who wrote one of the first books on [[Theory of relativity|relativity]] and co-edited two volumes of [[William Rowan Hamilton]]'s collected works.  He also served as President of [[University College Dublin]] between 1940 and 1947.<ref name=tutor/>

==Life and career==
[[File:Arthur W Conway plaque.jpg|thumb|Memorial plaque in [[Wexford]] town]]
Born in [[Wexford]], he received his early education in [[St Peter's College, Wexford]] and proceeded to enter old University College, Dublin in 1892. He received his BA degree from the [[Royal University of Ireland]] in 1896 with honours in [[Latin]], English, [[Mathematics]] and [[Natural Philosophy]]. In 1897, he received his MA degree with highest honours in mathematics and proceeded to [[Corpus Christi College, Oxford]], becoming University Scholar there in 1898, and studying under [[Augustus Love]].<ref name=tutor/>  Also in 1901, he was appointed to the professorship of [[Mathematical Physics]] in the old University College Dublin and held the chair until the creation of the new college in 1909 until 1940. He also taught for a short time at [[St. Patrick's College, Maynooth]].

He married Agnes Christina Bingham on 19 August 1903; they had three daughters and one son.<ref name=tutor>{{MacTutor Biography|id= Conway_Arthur}}</ref>

One of Conway's students was [[Éamon de Valera]], whom he introduced to Hamilton's [[quaternion]]s.<ref name=tutor/>  De Valera warmed to the subject and engaged in research of this novelty of [[abstract algebra]]. Later, when de Valera became Taoiseach (he was also subsequently [[President of Ireland]]), he called upon Conway while forming the [[Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies]].<ref>[http://www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/history/Biographies/De_Valera.html De Valera] School of Mathematics and Statistics
University of St Andrews, Scotland</ref>

Conway's earliest publications, dating back to 1903, were on the electromagnetic theory.  He is remembered for his application of [[biquaternion]] algebra to the [[special theory of relativity]], and in 1915 published a 43-page tract "Relativity" in Edinburgh. He published an article<ref>Arthur W. Conway (1911) "On the application of quaternions to some recent developments in electrical theory", ''[[Proceedings of the Royal Irish Academy]]'' 29 A:1–9 [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/108052#page/13/mode/1up BHL link] via [[Biodiversity Heritage Library]]</ref> in 1911, and in 1912 asserted priority over [[Ludwik Silberstein]], who also applied biquaternions to relativity.<ref>A.W. Conway (1912) "The quaternionic form of relativity", ''[[Philosophical Magazine]]'' (6) 24:208</ref> This claim was backed up by [[George Temple (mathematician)|George Temple]] in his book ''100 Years of Mathematics''.<ref>[[George Temple (mathematician)|George Temple]] (1981) ''100 Years of Mathematics: a personal viewpoint'', §6.6 "Quaternions in Relativity Theory", page 51, [[Springer-Verlag]] {{ISBN|0-387-91192-8}}</ref> In 1947 Conway put quaternions to use with rotations in hyperbolic space.<ref>A.W. Conway (1947) "Applicationsof quaternions to rotations in hyperbolic space", [[Proceedings of the Royal Society A]] 191:137–45</ref> The next year he published [[quantum mechanics]] applications<ref>A.W. Conway (1948) [http://www.casinapioiv.va/content/dam/accademia/pdf/acta12/acta12-conway.pdf "Quaternions and quantum mechanics"] Pontificia Academia Scientiarum, Acta Vol. XII-N.23, 1948</ref> which were referred to in a PhD thesis<ref>J. Lambek (1950) "Biquaternion vector fields over Minkowski space", PhD thesis, April 1950</ref> by [[J. Lambek]] in 1950.

In 1918, he was the [[Irish Parliamentary Party]] candidate in [[South Londonderry (UK Parliament constituency)|South Londonderry]] and in the [[National University of Ireland (constituency)|National University]], coming second in both.<ref>{{cite book|title=Parliamentary Election Results in Ireland, 1801–1922|editor-first=B.M.|editor-last=Walker|publisher=Royal Irish Academy|year=1978|location=Dublin|isbn=0901714127|pages=185–191}}</ref>

Arthur Conway continued his scholarship in the fields of mathematics and theoretical physics, and made a special study of [[William Rowan Hamilton]]. With [[John Lighton Synge|J. L. Synge]], he edited the first volume of Hamilton's mathematical papers<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Conway, A. W.|author2=Synge, J. L.|title=Letter to the Editor: Hamilton's Contributions to Geometrical Optics|journal=Nature|date=9 March 1929|volume=123|page=349|doi=10.1038/123349c0|bibcode=1929Natur.123..349C|doi-access=free}}</ref> and with A. J. McConnell he edited the second volume of Hamilton's mathematical papers.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Bourgin, D. G.|title=Review: ''The Mathematical Papers of Sir William Rowan Hamilton'', Vol. II|journal=Bull. Amer. Math. Soc.|year=1942|volume=48|issue=11|pages=813–818|url=https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/1942-48-11/S0002-9904-1942-07796-2/|doi=10.1090/s0002-9904-1942-07796-2|doi-access=free}}</ref> Conway was also active in college life, being appointed [[Registrar (education)|Registrar]], a position he occupied until his election as president in 1940.<ref>{{cite web |url = http://www.ucd.ie/archives/html/collections/conway-arthurw.html | publisher = UCD Archives | title = Arthur W. Conway | access-date = 29 August 2006 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20060825053929/http://www.ucd.ie/archives/html/collections/conway-arthurw.html| archive-date= 25 August 2006 | url-status= live}}</ref> He retired in 1947 from the presidency of UCD. In 1953, some of his writings were edited by J. McConnell for publication by the Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies.<ref>J. McConnell (1953) ''Selected Papers of Arthur William Conway'', Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies.</ref>

He was an Invited Speaker of the [[International Congress of Mathematicians|ICM]] in Toronto in 1924,<ref>{{cite book|author=Conway, A. W.|chapter=The mathematical works of Sir W. R. Hamilton|title=''In:'' Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians in Toronto, August 11–16. 1924|volume=2|page=984}}</ref> in 1932 in Zurich, and in 1936 in Oslo. He was elected President of the [[Royal Irish Academy]] from 1937 to 1940.

In October 1975, to mark the centenary of his birth, UCD hosted the AC Conway Memorial Mathematical Symposium.  Speakers included [[Roger Penrose]], [[Ian Sneddon]], and [[William B. Bonnor]].

In his obituary, [[E.T. Whittaker]] referred to Conway as the "most distinguished Irish Catholic man of science of his generation."<ref name="WhittakerObit"/>{{rp|329}}

==Books==
* 1915: [https://archive.org/details/cu31924001080682 Relativity], G. Bell & Sons (Edinburgh Mathematical Tracts No. 3) via [[Internet Archive]]
* 1931: ''The Mathematical Papers of Sir William Rowan Hamilton: Volume 1, Geometrical Optics'', Cambridge (edited with [[J L Synge]])
* 1940: ''The Mathematical Papers of Sir William Rowan Hamilton: Volume 2, Dynamics'', Cambridge (edited with J L Synge)
